newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan tries to dodge U.S. electoral mudslinging.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan tries to dodge U.S. electoral mudslinging.

text.p: Taiwan, suddenly under the hot U.S. political spotlight over possible illicit contributions to Bill Clinton's re-election campaign, is scrambling to avert damage to its hard-won reputation as Asia's new democracy.

Government and ruling Nationalist Party brass have vigorously denied a report in Hong Kong's Asiaweek magazine that a senior party official considered making a US$15 million contribution to the Democratic National Committee.
Accepting such a donation would be illegal under U.S. law and the U.S. Justice Department has launched an inquiry, although the legal implications for foreign donors are unclear.
Even President Lee Teng-hui, who doubles as Nationalist Party chairman, has denied that party business management chief Liu Tai-ying was authorised to make such a gift.

"This question absolutely doesn't exist," Lee said at a party central committee meeting on Wednesday. "This party has never made such a decision. I have never authorised Liu Tai-ying to do such a thing."

Underlying the denials is dread that Taiwan will be sullied with the political mud being slung by Democrat Clinton and his Republican challenger Bob Dole in the final days before the November 5 U.S. presidential election.
Dole has heaped scorn on Clinton -- and on his putative supporters in Taiwan and Indonesia -- in a bid to fuel popular doubt about the incumbent's fitness for a second term.
Taiwan Foreign Minister John Chang warned on Thursday that Taiwan must not be made a "scapegoat" in the U.S. debate over campaign contributions from foreign sources.

Taiwan's China Times, in a commentary echoed in other newspapers, warned that miscalculations could undermine crucial U.S. sympathy for Taiwan, which counts on U.S. diplomatic and even military support in its its rivalry with communist China.

"Taiwan's image has been severely damaged and this has caused a diplomatic crisis," the China Times said. "Since Taipei and Washington have no official diplomatic ties, such damage is especially severe."
Since the lifting of martial law in 1987 ended four decades of tough Nationalist authoritarianism and legalised a political opposition, Taiwan's fledgling democracy has flourished.
The island seated its first popularly elected parliament in 1992 and in March gave Lee his first democratic mandate in the first popular presidential election in Chinese history.
Fistfights in parliament sometimes mar the image, but the 21 million people of Taiwan are proud of their pluralist system, free press and speech and unfettered political debate.
Taipei's biggest headache, the China Times said, would be to figure out how to handle the crisis and rebuild Taiwan's image -- whether a $15 million donation was made or not.
Taiwan's drive to break free of Beijing-imposed isolation, including lobbying of foreign governments, was proper but must be pursued carefully and with close supervision, it said.

Significantly, there appeared to be broad consensus in the ruling party, the opposition and popular media that because of its lack of diplomatic ties with all but 30 nations, Taiwan should use its huge wealth to build political bridges.

"Taiwan has a lot of money. But when we make political contributions to the United States, we must consider whether they violate U.S. law," said lawmaker Tsai Ming-hsien of the main opposition Democratic Progressive Party.
